title: "One call, end to end"
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use("styles/mint.mplstyle")
```

A `Scenario` is a description of a place and a plan. The place is fixed by the survey and
the entomology; the plan is whatever changes at the campaign. `run_scenarios` takes a list
of those descriptions and returns a table. The two objects are plain dataclasses,
importable from either `estimint` or `estimint.scenarios`.

```python
from estimint import run_scenarios
from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget
```

## The seven required fields

These have no defaults and must be given for every scenario. Together they describe the
setting as it stands, before anything is done to it.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | A label. It is echoed into the results and is how you index them afterwards. |
| `res_use` | Pyrethroid resistance, 0 (fully susceptible) to 1 (fully resistant). |
| `Q0` | Human blood index, 0 to 1. |
| `phi` | Share of bites taken while people are in bed. Enters the emulator as `phi_bednets`. |
| `seasonal` | 0 for perennial transmission, 1 for strongly seasonal. |
| `irs` | IRS coverage currently in place. Enters the emulator as `irs_use`. |
| `eir_target` | An `EirTarget`. How transmission intensity is specified. |

Three of these are renamed on the way in. `phi` becomes `phi_bednets` and `irs` becomes
`irs_use`. `res_use` is not a covariate at all, being consumed by the `dn0` curves and
never reaching the emulator. What the emulator sees is the
[twelve static covariates](../05-statemint/covariates.qmd).

## The three input modes

`EirTarget(input_value, input_mode)` says what quantity you are handing over. The emulator
only ever runs from an EIR, so the mode decides how much work estiMINT does first.

| Mode | You supply | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `"prevalence"` | Under-5 parasite prevalence in [0.005, 0.80] | estiMINT inverts it to an EIR with the XGBoost prevalence model. |
| `"eir"` | An EIR, infectious bites per person per year | Used directly. No inversion. |
| `"hbr"` | A human biting rate | Converted to an EIR through the HBR model. |

Use `"prevalence"` when the evidence is a cross-sectional survey, as it is for the district
worked through here. Use `"eir"` when the EIR is already in hand, or is the quantity you are
sweeping over. Use `"hbr"` when the evidence is entomological.

`mosquito_delta` only applies to `"prevalence"`. Supplied alongside an `"eir"` or `"hbr"`
input it is silently ignored, because there is no prevalence-to-EIR step for it to modify.
The mechanism is set out in
[Mosquito density and EIR](../04-estimint/mosquito-density.qmd).

## The ten defaulted fields

Everything else defaults. Every default is zero or `None`.

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `py_only` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-only nets. |
| `py_pbo` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-PBO nets. |
| `py_pyrrole` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-pyrrole nets. |
| `py_ppf` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-PPF nets. |
| `mosquito_delta` | `0.0` | Proportional change in mosquito density. Must be > −1. |
| `itn_future` | `0.0` | Net coverage from the campaign. |
| `net_type_future` | `None` | Net product from the campaign. |
| `irs_future` | `0.0` | IRS coverage from the campaign. |
| `routine` | `0.0` | Routine (continuous) net distribution from the campaign. |
| `lsm` | `0.0` | Larval source management coverage from the campaign. |

The first four are the current net mix. Their coverages are summed to give `itn_use` and
their `dn0` values averaged to give `dn0_use`. The rest describe the campaign. `routine` and
`lsm` carry no `_future` suffix but belong to the campaign all the same. Like `dn0_future`,
`itn_future` and `irs_future`, they are held at zero for every timestep before day 3285, and
take their supplied value only from the campaign onwards.

::: {.callout-important}
## Future coverage must be set explicitly

If `itn_future` is 0 or `net_type_future` is `None`, then `dn0_future` and `itn_future` are
both set to 0, and the nets are **withdrawn** at the campaign. `irs_future` behaves the same
way and does not inherit from `irs`.

To hold an intervention steady you must restate it. A district with pyrethroid-only nets
at 0.70 that intends to keep them
needs `itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only"` written out in full. Omit it, and
the district has been modelled as abandoning nets. The rebound in the trajectory is then
real output from a scenario nobody intended.
:::

## One call

The district has measured under-5 prevalence 0.45, pyrethroid resistance 0.30,
pyrethroid-only nets at 0.70 coverage, perennial transmission and no IRS. The plan is to
switch those nets to PBO at the same coverage.

```{python}
from estimint import run_scenarios
from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget

pbo = Scenario(
    name="PBO",
    res_use=0.30,
    Q0=0.85,
    phi=0.80,
    seasonal=0.0,
    irs=0.0,
    eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"),
    py_only=0.70,                        # the nets in place now
    itn_future=0.70,                     # the campaign
    net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo",
)

res = run_scenarios([pbo])
res.shape
```

The frame that comes back has one row and twenty-three columns.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Net type names

`net_type_future` accepts `"pyrethroid_pbo"` or the short alias `"py_pbo"`. It does not
accept `"pyrethroid-pbo"`. A hyphen raises `ValueError: unknown net type`.
:::

## The returned columns

The returned frame is one row per scenario. Its columns fall into four groups.

The first group is **what you asked for, resolved**. It gives the current net mix reduced to
a single product name, together with the product used in the campaign.

```{python}
res[["name", "input_mode", "net", "net_future"]]
```

With no campaign nets, `net_future` comes back as the string `"none"` rather than a missing
value.

The second group is **the covariates the emulator actually saw**. These are derived rather
than echoed. Read them back to check that the scenario that ran is the one you built.

```{python}
res[[
    "dn0_use", "itn_use", "irs_use",
    "dn0_future", "itn_future", "irs_future",
    "routine", "lsm", "seasonal",
]]
```

`dn0_use` is the usage-weighted `dn0` of the current mix, and `itn_use` the sum of its
coverages. `dn0_future` is the `dn0` of the campaign product at the same resistance. `lsm`
is not always the `lsm` you passed. `run_scenarios` folds PPF net coverage into effective
larval source management before the emulator runs, under the rule set out in
[Pipeline architecture](../07-under-the-hood/architecture.qmd).

The third group is **transmission intensity**. `eir_baseline` is what the inversion produced
from the measured prevalence. `eir_final` is that EIR after `mosquito_delta` has been
applied, and equals `eir_baseline` when the delta is zero.

```{python}
res[["eir_baseline", "mosquito_delta", "eir_final", "hbr_baseline", "hbr_new"]]
```

`hbr_baseline` and `hbr_new` are `NaN` here, and will be for most scenarios. They are only
populated when a prevalence input is combined with a non-zero `mosquito_delta`. The HBR is
an intermediate in that calculation and is not otherwise computed.

The fourth group is **outcomes**. `prev_y9` is prevalence at the campaign and should be
close to the 0.45 that was supplied, the small gap being the round trip through the
inversion and the emulator. `prev_endline` and `cases_endline` are the last window of the
horizon, three years later.

```{python}
res[["prev_y9", "prev_endline", "cases_endline"]]
```

## The trajectories

The last two columns, `prevalence` and `cases`, are not scalars. Each cell holds the full
trajectory as a 157-element NumPy array, stored inside the DataFrame rather than unrolled
into a tidy long table.

```{python}
import numpy as np

prev = np.asarray(res.loc[0, "prevalence"])
cases = np.asarray(res.loc[0, "cases"])

type(prev), prev.shape, prev.dtype
```

This is convenient for a five-row grid and awkward for anything else. The frame cannot be
written to CSV as it stands. Any comparison across scenarios has to reach into the cells
first. [Exporting results](exporting.qmd) deals with both.

The 157 windows are a property of the emulator, so read the grid off the artefact rather
than hard-coding it. `preload_models` returns the three estiMINT XGBoost models and the two
stateMINT artefacts. These are the same objects `run_scenarios` uses internally. Calling it
once up front also warms the caches and pulls the weights from HuggingFace before the first
run rather than during it.

```{python}
from estimint import preload_models

xgb_models, artifacts = preload_models()
cfg = artifacts["prevalence"].preprocessing_config

n_steps = cfg["n_steps"]
window = cfg["window_size"]
start = cfg["model_start_day"]
campaign = cfg["intervention_day"]

abs_t = start + window * np.arange(n_steps)
years = (abs_t - campaign) / 365
idx_y9 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(abs_t - campaign)))

n_steps, window, start, campaign, idx_y9
```

`idx_y9` is the index of the window in which the campaign falls. Everything before it is
baseline. Everything from it onwards is response. In `years` the campaign sits at zero.

```{python}
float(years[0]), float(years[idx_y9]), float(years[-1])
```

The horizon covers three years of baseline and three years of response. A trajectory can
then be taken out of a cell and plotted against that axis in two lines.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Prevalence under the PBO campaign. The dashed line marks the campaign at year 0; everything to its left is the run-up under the nets already in place."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of under-five prevalence from three years before the campaign to three years after. Before the campaign prevalence dips to about 0.29 and climbs back to about 0.46. After the campaign it falls to about 0.26 within a year, then rises again to about 0.47 by the end of the horizon."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(years, prev, color="#00d4aa")
ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Years since campaign")
ax.set_ylabel("Prevalence (under 5)")
ax.set_ylim(0, None)
plt.show()
```

The three years to the left of the line are the model's run-up to the campaign under the
nets already in place. The prevalence you supply is prevalence *at the campaign*, not at the
start of the horizon. The value to check against your input is `prev_y9`, not the level
anywhere in the run-up.

After the campaign, prevalence reaches its minimum about a year in and rises again over the
rest of the horizon. Whether it rebounds less far than the alternatives cannot be answered
from one scenario.

## The weights repository

Both `run_scenarios` and `preload_models` take an `hf_repo` argument, defaulting to
`"dide-ic/stateMINT"`.

```python
res = run_scenarios([pbo], hf_repo="dide-ic/stateMINT")
```

Change it to run against a fork or a local snapshot of the weights. `run_scenarios` tracks
whatever `main` currently points at in that repository and exposes no revision pin. If an
analysis has to be reproducible years from now, record the weight version alongside the
results, or drive the emulator directly with a pinned `revision` as in
[Calling the emulator](../05-statemint/the-emulator.qmd).
